planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Okumidori is a late-budding Japanese cultivar valued for producing high-grade sencha and gyokuro with a deep green color.

directions: Bred in Shizuoka Prefecture and registered in Japan in 1966, Okumidori has become the second most widely planted tea cultivar in the country after Yabukita, prized by growers for the deep emerald color and rounded, mellow sweetness it lends to shade-grown gyokuro and high-grade sencha. Its late budbreak, roughly a week behind Yabukita, spreads out the spring harvest window and helps growers avoid losing an entire crop to a single late frost. The cultivar's name translates roughly to "deep green," a nod to the intense color of both the living leaf and the finished liquor. Grow it under the same acidic, humus-rich conditions recommended for other Camellia sinensis cultivars, and prune into a rounded hedge to encourage the dense flush growth needed for hand or machine plucking.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products
National Agriculture and Food Research Organization (Japan)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Tie Luo Han is best suited to USDA zones 8-10.

directions: Tie Luo Han, or "Iron Arhat," is one of the Wuyi Mountains' Si Da Ming Cong ("Four Great Bushes"), the small group of heirloom rock-tea cultivars that, alongside Da Hong Pao, Bai Jiguan, and Shui Jin Gui, anchor the most prized yancha oolongs of Fujian Province. Local legend traces the original bushes to Huiyuan Cliff and credits the tea with folk-medicinal uses long before it became famous as a premium oolong source. Like its Wuyi siblings it performs best in mineral-rich, well-drained mountain soils with partial shade, developing the mineral, roasted "rock rhyme" character prized in traditionally charcoal-fired processing. Harvest semi-mature leaves typical of oolong production rather than the youngest buds used for green tea.
sources: Tea Research Institute, Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Bai Jiguan is best suited to USDA zones 8-10.

directions: Bai Jiguan, meaning "White Cockscomb," is named for its distinctive pale yellow-green new growth, which emerges noticeably lighter than the surrounding foliage and curls somewhat like a rooster's comb — the palest-leaved of the four historic Wuyi Si Da Ming Cong cultivars grown alongside Da Hong Pao, Tie Luo Han, and Shui Jin Gui. Its naturally lower chlorophyll content in young leaves is said to give the finished oolong a lighter, more delicate character than the deeper, more heavily roasted styles typical of other Wuyi rock teas. Grow it in the same mineral-rich, well-drained mountain soil and partial shade favored by other Wuyi cultivars, and expect a somewhat less vigorous, slower-growing bush than its siblings. Traditional processing uses a lighter roast than Da Hong Pao to preserve its comparatively delicate aromatics.
sources: Tea Research Institute, Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences

common_name: Shui Jin Gui Tea (Golden Water Turtle)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Shui Jin Gui is best suited to USDA zones 8-10.

directions: Shui Jin Gui, or "Golden Water Turtle," rounds out the Wuyi Mountains' Si Da Ming Cong alongside Da Hong Pao, Tie Luo Han, and Bai Jiguan, and takes its name from a legend describing an original bush's leaves gleaming like a golden turtle after rain. It is noted among the four for comparatively high yield and vigor and for a lighter, sweeter, more floral cup than the deeply roasted Da Hong Pao style, making it a popular everyday yancha oolong as well as a collector's cultivar. As with the other Wuyi rock-tea cultivars, it performs best in the mineral-rich, well-drained mountain soils and partial shade of its native terrain, developing more pronounced yan yun "rock rhyme" character with age. Harvest semi-mature leaves for oolong-style processing, expecting the multiple roasting rounds typical of traditional Wuyi production.
sources: Tea Research Institute, Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Dove Wings is an Alec Gray-bred Cyclamineus hybrid with swept-back cream petals surrounding a soft yellow trumpet that fades paler with age.

directions: Bred by the pioneering miniature-daffodil hybridizer Alec Gray and introduced in the late 1940s, Dove Wings crosses Narcissus cyclamineus with a trumpet parent to produce creamy white, reflexed petals swept back from a soft lemon-yellow trumpet that pales further as the flower ages, giving the two-tone look that inspired its name. It is an early, reliable perennializer that naturalizes well in light shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs, where it can be left undisturbed for years. Its Cyclamineus parentage gives it good vigor and a long-lived, multiplying clump habit compared with many hybrid daffodils. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom without braiding or cutting it, since it recharges the bulb for next year's flowers.

common_name: Charity May Daffodil (Soft Yellow Cyclamineus Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Charity May is an early Cyclamineus hybrid with softly reflexed, all-yellow flowers on a compact, weather-resistant plant.

directions: Another Alec Gray introduction from the same mid-twentieth-century breeding program that produced Dove Wings, Charity May bears solid soft-yellow flowers with the characteristic swept-back Cyclamineus petals, opening slightly later than many of its siblings and standing up well to spring wind and rain. Its short, sturdy stems and early bloom make it a dependable choice for rock gardens, containers, and the front of mixed borders where taller daffodils would overwhelm the scale. Like other Cyclamineus hybrids it multiplies readily and can be left undisturbed for many years. Let the foliage yellow and die back completely before removing it so the bulb can store energy for the following spring.

common_name: Toto Daffodil (White Cyclamineus with Pale Yellow Cup)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Toto is a dwarf Cyclamineus daffodil with white, swept-back petals and a small pale yellow cup, occasionally producing more than one flower per stem.

directions: Toto is a compact Cyclamineus hybrid daffodil bearing white, wind-blown petals around a small, pale primrose-yellow cup, sometimes carrying two flowers on a single stem where most Cyclamineus types carry only one. Its short stature and early bloom time make it a good choice for rock gardens, alpine troughs, and the front of a border, where its distinctive reflexed form stands out at close range. It is a vigorous perennializer that slowly builds into dense clumps over the years without division. Deadhead spent flowers if desired for tidiness, but always allow the strap-like foliage to die back naturally to recharge the bulb.

common_name: Foundling Daffodil (White Cyclamineus with Rose-Pink Cup)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Foundling is a Cyclamineus hybrid with reflexed white petals surrounding a distinctive rose-pink cup that deepens in cool spring weather.

directions: Foundling combines the swept-back Cyclamineus form with a rose-pink cup that intensifies in cool spring weather, one of the earliest pink-cupped daffodils bred small enough for the rock garden rather than the border. The pink pigment in daffodil cups is famously unstable and fades in strong sun or warmth, so the deepest color shows in a partly shaded, cool site or during an unusually cool spring. Its dwarf scale and early flowering pair well with taller pink-cupped large-cup daffodils for a season-long pink theme. Leave the foliage to die back naturally after bloom, and expect slow, steady multiplication into established clumps over the years.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Tresamble is a Triandrus hybrid typically carrying three or more nodding, creamy white flowers per stem.

directions: Bred by Northern Irish hybridizer W.J. Dunlop and long a favorite among Triandrus daffodils, Tresamble carries clusters of three to six small, nodding, creamy white flowers per stem with the gracefully reflexed petals typical of Narcissus triandrus parentage. Its multi-flowered habit and fine, wiry stems give it a delicate, informal look well suited to naturalizing in light woodland shade or a mixed spring border. Like other Triandrus hybrids it tends to prefer cooler summers and can be shorter-lived in the hottest, most humid climates. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after flowering, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Trena is an early-flowering Triandrus hybrid with nodding, soft yellow blooms on wiry stems.

directions: Trena is an early Triandrus hybrid daffodil producing one or two nodding, clear yellow flowers per stem, with the gracefully reflexed petals and pendant carriage that define the Triandrus group. Its early bloom time makes it a useful companion to later triandrus and jonquilla types for extending the naturalized-daffodil season. The wiry stems and dainty flower size suit it to rock gardens and the front of borders rather than mass bedding display. As with other Triandrus daffodils, allow the foliage to die back naturally and avoid disturbing established clumps, which slowly increase over several years.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Petrel is a Triandrus hybrid bred by Oregon hybridizer Grant Mitsch, typically bearing several small white flowers per stem.

directions: Bred by American daffodil hybridizer Grant Mitsch, Petrel carries clusters of several small, pure white, nodding flowers per stem, taller and more floriferous than many Triandrus cultivars while retaining the group's characteristic reflexed petals and graceful, pendant carriage. Its clustered white blooms show well against dark mulch or evergreen groundcovers in a woodland-edge planting. It naturalizes readily in climates with cool springs and moderate summers, multiplying into larger clumps over time. Let the foliage yellow and die back completely before cutting it back so the bulb can store energy for next year.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Kokopelli is a vigorous jonquilla hybrid bearing clusters of small, fragrant, deep yellow flowers on each stem.

directions: Kokopelli is a jonquilla hybrid from the Oregon breeding program of Grant Mitsch and Elise Havens, producing clusters of up to five or six small, fragrant, rich golden-yellow flowers per stem well above narrow, rush-like jonquil foliage. Its heat tolerance and reliable perennializing make it one of the more popular modern jonquillas for warmer climates where many hybrid daffodils struggle to return. The strong, sweet fragrance carries well in the garden and makes it a good choice for cut-flower bouquets. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom, since jonquilla types recharge slowly and resent premature removal of their leaves.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Baby Boomer is a miniature jonquilla hybrid producing clusters of two to five tiny, fragrant, deep yellow flowers per stem.

directions: Baby Boomer is a diminutive jonquilla hybrid from the Mitsch Daffodils breeding program, packing clusters of two to five small, fragrant, golden-yellow flowers onto short, sturdy stems well under a foot tall. Its miniature scale, heavy multi-flowered display, and reliable perennializing have made it one of the most widely planted small jonquillas in recent decades, popular for containers, rock gardens, and the front of borders. The narrow, grassy foliage and compact habit keep the planting tidy even after bloom. Allow the foliage to die back naturally without braiding or cutting it, and expect clumps to bulk up steadily over a few seasons.

common_name: Hillstar Daffodil (Pale Yellow Jonquilla with Cream Cup)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Hillstar is a jonquilla hybrid with pale lemon-yellow petals surrounding a slightly darker, flattened cup, usually one to two flowers per stem.

directions: Bred by Grant Mitsch, Hillstar produces soft lemon-yellow flowers with a slightly deeper yellow, flattened cup, usually one or two per stem, on a compact plant with the fine, rush-like foliage typical of jonquilla parentage. Its pale, understated coloring and light fragrance make it a good companion for stronger-colored daffodils in a mixed spring planting. It is a reliable, long-lived perennializer that tolerates warmer climates better than many non-jonquilla hybrids. Let the foliage die back naturally after flowering, and leave clumps undisturbed to increase over time.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Sundial is a miniature jonquilla hybrid with small, bright yellow, flat-faced flowers on very short stems.

directions: Sundial is a true miniature jonquilla hybrid, standing well under eight inches tall and bearing small, bright, uniformly golden-yellow flowers with a flattened, star-like face typical of the smallest jonquilla types. Its diminutive scale makes it especially well suited to alpine troughs, rock gardens, and small containers where full-sized daffodils would be out of proportion. It is a vigorous, early perennializer within its class and multiplies reliably when left undisturbed. Allow the narrow, grassy foliage to die back completely after bloom before any cleanup.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Precocious is a large-cupped daffodil with a pure white perianth and a ruffled, rose-pink cup that deepens in cool weather.

directions: Precocious pairs a bright white perianth with a large, ruffled, rose-pink cup, one of the earlier-blooming pink-cupped large-cup daffodils bred to bring pink color to the front of the daffodil season rather than mid- or late spring. As with all pink daffodils, the intensity of the color depends heavily on temperature — cool, overcast weather during bloom produces the deepest rose tones, while a warm spring can fade the cup toward pale peach. Its sturdy, standard-height stems make it a strong choice for cutting as well as border display. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom to recharge the bulb for the following year.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Pink Charm is a classic mid-twentieth-century large-cupped daffodil with a pure white perianth and a flared cup that opens yellow and matures to salmon-pink.

directions: A classic among pink-cupped daffodils, Pink Charm pairs broad, pure white petals with a flared cup that opens pale yellow and gradually deepens to a warm salmon-pink as the flower matures, one of the earliest widely grown pink daffodils to reliably hold its color in the garden rather than fading quickly. Decades after its introduction it remains a benchmark cultivar against which many newer pink-cupped daffodils are still compared. Grow it alongside earlier pink Cyclamineus and later large-cup types for a season-long pink theme in the spring border. Leave the foliage to die back completely and undisturbed after bloom, since large-cup daffodils take several weeks after flowering to recharge.

common_name: Sir Winston Churchill Daffodil (Fragrant Double Tazetta)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Sir Winston Churchill is a fully double tazetta daffodil bearing clusters of three or more fragrant, creamy white flowers flecked with orange-red per stem.

directions: Sir Winston Churchill carries clusters of three to five fragrant, fully double flowers per stem, creamy white petals flecked with orange-red at the center, giving a ruffled, almost rose-like appearance quite unlike a typical trumpet daffodil. Its tazetta parentage brings strong, sweet fragrance and a lower winter-chill requirement than most double daffodils, letting it perennialize better than many other doubles in milder climates. The multi-headed habit makes each stem showy enough for cutting on its own. Let the foliage die back naturally after bloom rather than braiding or removing it early, and leave clumps undisturbed to bulk up over a few seasons.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; White Lion is a fully double daffodil with creamy white outer petals surrounding an inner cluster of shorter pale yellow segments.

directions: White Lion produces large, fully double flowers with broad, creamy white outer petals surrounding a dense inner cluster of shorter, pale primrose-yellow segments, giving a full, peony-like form on a standard-height stem. Unlike doubles bred primarily from warm-climate tazetta ancestry, White Lion descends from trumpet and large-cup daffodils and is correspondingly more cold-hardy, performing well as far north as USDA zone 3. Its long-lasting, showy blooms make it a popular choice for both garden display and cutting. Allow the foliage to die back naturally and completely after flowering, since double daffodils can be a bit slower than singles to rebuild bloom-size bulbs.
